mathematical_review: All nominal and real rates share a period length. Exact gross-factor Fisher accounting is separated from log-rate identities, expected log returns and approximate or maintained linear behavioral equations. Ordinary percentage changes are not silently identified with log points.

IS is derived by substituting consumption and investment into the closed-economy goods condition; LM is a portfolio-demand condition. Positive determinant gives algebraic uniqueness, while nonnegative quantities, capacity and rate restrictions are checked separately. Fixed money and an accommodated rate peg give different multipliers. The borrowing-premium and expected-inflation channels enter real investment costs with opposite signs.

Current government consumption and capital formation use explicit accounting categories. Debt-financed short-run spending comparisons do not claim to solve later taxes, debt service, lifetime welfare or fiscal solvency. There is no mechanical reserve/deposit multiplier.

AD is derived at fixed nominal M with real balances M/P, not by silently holding both money and the policy rate fixed. The supply relation concerns the current price level and predetermined reference price. Positive-root and monotonicity arguments establish the unique admissible intersection, and dated price ratios distinguish a one-time increase from persistent inflation.

The finite real benchmark includes current consumption/investment resources, full depreciation, positive consumption and terminal exhaustion. Its strictly concave log objective has a unique global interior optimum. Future productivity cancellation is derived as a special log/multiplicative result and is not generalized to arbitrary preferences, labor or financing.

The finite NK system is maintained directly as a reduced three-equation model, with forward coefficient separate from the real-model utility weight or a common DSGE calibration. Shock-specific natural output/rate definitions, a zero total inflation target, forward information dates and finite terminal conditions are supplied before solving.

At each date a positive denominator gives the free-rate candidate. At a floor, quantities are recomputed and the requested-rate inequality is checked. Monotone intersection proves existence/uniqueness for the finite input and each branch, including equality; backward induction uses the explicit terminal values. No infinite-horizon determinacy, horizon-uniform bound or quantitative large-gap approximation claim is made.

Announced future demand, supply and policy changes affect current forecasts and equilibrium. An unanticipated revision uses a different information history; a stochastic extension would need a conditional distribution at each node. The chapter does not use perfect foresight as a synonym for rational expectations.

One-date policy loss is a stated quadratic criterion in squared log points, not a claimed measured welfare function. Completing the square proves globality with the rate-implied upper bound on output. A feedback rule and the separately optimized choice are distinguished, as are one-date discretion and a multi-date commitment problem.

Observational equivalence is constructed under identical demand/inflation coefficients. Rates, forecasts, natural benchmarks, policy operating rules and external identification are needed to distinguish mechanisms. A zero natural gap neither means unchanged output nor guarantees an efficient natural allocation.

limitations: Original synthetic maintained models and exact computations are not empirical calibration or external academic certification.
Finite reduced NK equations do not establish a full common-household DSGE, infinite-horizon equilibrium selection or approximation accuracy for large gaps.
The fixed-labor real benchmark does not model endogenous employment, heterogeneous risk, financial frictions or complete business-cycle facts.
Computational checks supplement analytic arguments; they cannot establish empirical identification, appropriate welfare weights or policy effectiveness in an actual economy.
